facts.text: On this date in 1945, Vidkun Quisling was sentenced to death in Norway — his surname had already entered English dictionaries as a common noun for 'traitor' before he was executed.
On this date in 1960, Ethiopia's Abebe Bikila won the Olympic marathon in Rome — barefoot — becoming the first Black African to claim Olympic gold.
More people live inside a circle drawn around Dhaka with a 4,000km radius than outside it.
Canada has more lakes than every other country on Earth combined, containing roughly 60% of the world's fresh surface water.
Manila is the most densely populated city on Earth — over 111,000 people per square kilometer, denser than any neighborhood in New York or Tokyo.

On this day in 1998, a single day's panic selling erased $1.5 trillion in global market value as the Long-Term Capital Management crisis peaked — a hedge fund nearly took down the world's financial system.
On Sept 10, 2001, the NYSE traded a then-record 1.4 billion shares. The next session wouldn't open for six days.

The Dutch East India Company, often called the first publicly traded firm, once had a market cap equivalent to roughly $8 trillion in today's dollars — larger than Apple, Microsoft, and Saudi Aramco combined.
Berkshire Hathaway's Class A shares have never split. One share currently costs over $700,000, making it the highest-priced stock on any major exchange by design.
The S&P 500's ten best trading days in any given decade typically account for the majority of its total returns — missing them by sitting in cash is how most investors actually underperform.
On this date in 1974, the Arecibo Message was broadcast toward globular cluster M13 — 25,000 light-years away. Any reply would arrive around the year 52,000.
On September 10, 1898, Empress Elisabeth of Austria was assassinated with a needle file so thin her wound didn't bleed for minutes — a delay that made survival seem possible.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere the size of a city. A teaspoon of its material would weigh roughly a billion tons on Earth.
Your body contains roughly 37 trillion cells, yet only about 200 distinct cell types exist — the same basic toolkit, endlessly redeployed to build everything from corneas to heartbeats.
Time passes measurably faster at your head than at your feet. Over a lifetime, the difference accumulates to roughly 90 nanoseconds — relativity made personal.
On this day in 1846, Elias Howe patented the sewing machine — older than the safety pin, the paper bag, and the modern toilet, all invented after it.
Oxford University was teaching students before the Aztec Empire existed. Oxford: 1096. Aztecs founded Tenochtitlan: 1325.
On this day in 1608, John Smith's map of Virginia was published — the same year Shakespeare was writing Coriolanus and Galileo was first pointing his telescope at the sky.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid. She died 30 BC. The pyramid: 2560 BC. Apollo 11: 1969.
On this day in 1897, the first speeding ticket in history was issued in Paddington, England. The driver was doing 8 mph in a 2 mph zone.
**Hiraeth** (Welsh): a longing for a home you cannot return to — or one that never existed. Untranslatable into English, it fuses homesickness, grief, and nostalgia into a single ache.
**Sonder** first appeared in John Koenig's *Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows* (2012), not ancient texts. It means realizing every passerby lives a life as vivid and complex as your own.
**Apricity** is the warmth of winter sun on your skin. The word existed in English by 1623, then quietly vanished — leaving us no single word for one of life's small reliefs.
On this date in 1897, the word **'automobile'** was formally endorsed by *The New York Times* over rivals 'motocycle' and 'horseless carriage.' The editors called it 'the best' option. It stuck.

**Vellichor** shares its root feel with 'melancholy' — but it was coined in 2013. On September 10, 2013, Koenig published it: the strange wistfulness of used bookshops, haunted by lives you'll never know.

On this date in 2017, China's central bank declared ICOs illegal and ordered all funds returned to investors — triggering a 30% ETH price drop that recovered within six weeks as capital fled to non-Chinese exchanges.
On this date in 2022, Ethereum's Merge went live at epoch 144896, cutting the network's energy consumption by ~99.95% without interrupting a single block or breaking any running smart contract.
Bitcoin's smallest unit, the satoshi, wasn't named by Satoshi Nakamoto — the community coined the term in 2010, and it took years before it appeared in any official Bitcoin documentation.

The DAO hack of 2016 didn't exploit a flaw in Ethereum itself — it exploited a reentrancy bug in third-party Solidity code, a distinction the Ethereum Foundation was careful to maintain throughout the subsequent hard fork debate.

Ordinals inscriptions store data directly in Bitcoin transaction witnesses, a loophole enabled by SegWit's block weight rules — Bitcoin Core developers knew the possibility existed but considered it economically irrational at the time.
On this date in 2009, ImageNet launched publicly — the 3.2M-image dataset whose 2012 competition result would trigger the deep learning era three years later.
On this date in 2019, OpenAI released GPT-2's full 1.5B-parameter model after a staged rollout it called too dangerous, a decision widely mocked once the model proved unremarkable.

Transformers were invented to translate sentences, not to predict text. The 'Attention Is All You Need' authors expected their architecture to live inside encoder-decoder pipelines, not become the backbone of general intelligence research.
Training GPT-4 is estimated to have consumed more electricity than 1,000 US households use in a year — and inference, run continuously at scale, likely dwarfs that figure annually.
AlphaFold 2 predicted structures for ~200 million proteins in 2022. The entire prior history of experimental crystallography had solved roughly 190,000.
